The density curve using the marginal.hyperpar call gives a smooth curvelike this

parts:
inla.posterior.sample() is mainly intented for the latent field as for
the hyperparameters it use the integration points (hence the
hyperparameter simulations will be discrete)

> r = inla(y ~ 1, data=data.frame(y=0),
control.compute=list(config=TRUE))
> xx = inla.posterior.sample(1000, r)
> thetas = inla.posterior.sample.eval(function() theta, xx)
> unique(thetas[1,])
[1] 120.9983251 519.7477981 1550.7887175 4627.1396540
9590.0143518
[6] 19875.8589853 28845.9580098 41864.3186248 73195.2026123
127973.8417213



if you only want the hyperparmeters, then use inla.hyperpar.sample

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] INLA random effect posterior distribution curve
parts:
On Wed, 2022-12-14 at 08:30 -0800, ChooChoo JC wrote:
> Hi  Håvard,
>
> Thank you for your prompt response.
>
> So you meant that, instead of inla.posterior.sample$hyperpar, I should
> use inla.hyperpar.sample to sample for the hyperparameters. If I use
> that, would be resulted density curve be a good reference?

correct. you'll get essentially get the marginals back


r=inla(y~1,data=data.frame(y=0), control.compute=list(config=TRUE))
xx=inla.hyperpar.sample(10000, r)

hist(xx[,1], n=300, prob=TRUE)

p = exp(seq(0,log(150000), len=10000))
lines(p, inla.dmarginal(p, r$marginals.hyperpar[[1]]), lwd=4)


its better though to show the hyperparameter in the internal scale, like
log(prec), this is given in r$internal.marginals.hyperpar[[1]])

and you can add an option for this in hyperpar.sample

--
Håvard Rue
he...@r-inla.org

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] INLA random effect posterior distribution curve
parts:
for that example

thetas = inla.hyperpar.sample(100, r)

will sample precisions (for the likelihood terms)

while

thetas = inla.hyperpar.sample(100, r, intern=TRUE)

will sample log(precisions)
